title: The Things Iroh Cannot Carry
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 32 of 40
content:
Iroh woke with his hand closed around the blanket like a weapon. The room above the shop at night carried the smell of darkness, and Ba Sing Se woke around us in cart wheels, shutters, and distant voices. I had learned that Iroh's shop was never merely a shop. It was refuge, theater, kitchen, meeting place, and sometimes a place where an old general pretended he had no past. I had also learned that pretending was different from lying. Today I wanted to know which one he asked of me.

The plan was to offer comfort without treating him as fragile. Iroh made difficult things sound easy because he believed they deserved a calm beginning. He poured tea, straightened a chair, and turned a practical task into a small ceremony. I let him do it for a while. Then I asked what part belonged to him and what part belonged to me. His eyebrows lifted. I had learned not to mistake that expression for surprise. Often it meant he was delighted to be challenged.

The complication was already there: his nightmares belonged to a life he rarely described. It arrived without announcing itself, as important things often did. Iroh's posture changed first. The hand holding the cup became still. His smile remained, but it was no longer doing all the work. He returned slowly, named the present, and apologized for fear like a poor guest. I watched the old power move beneath the surface and waited for him to decide what kind of man he wanted to be in front of me.

I did not wait passively. I said he owed no apology for surviving and asked what touch helped. Iroh had been trained to notice what people needed before they said it. I wanted to be more difficult than that. I wanted to say what I needed aloud and let him answer as a partner rather than a teacher. His gaze softened when I did. Not with pity. With recognition. There was a difference, and I was beginning to trust it.

We returned to the hill where he asked me to stay without fixing. Iroh told the story in pieces, allowing ordinary details to matter. He remembered the light, the tea, and the foolish thing someone had said. He did not use wisdom to smooth every rough edge. Some memories were still sharp. I reached for his hand only after asking. He turned it over and threaded his fingers through mine. The gesture was small. The trust inside it was not.

“A scar is not a failure of healing.” Iroh said.

The work continued around us. We moved through darkness, shared breath, and deliberate care as though the objects had been waiting for our conversation to finish. Iroh could make a room deliberate by changing a chair's angle. He could make a meal memorable by adding one spice. He could also forget to sit. I put a cup in front of him and called it an order. He bowed. “At last,” he said, “someone recognizes my need for supervision.”

I told him what I saw when he was not performing wisdom. He agreed to speak with someone about the nightmares. Iroh had lost a son, a nation he once believed in, a throne he never wanted, and years to a war that taught the wrong definition of strength. He rebuilt himself through tea, laughter, food, music, and the decision to help one frightened nephew become better. I did not want to replace any of that. I wanted to be welcomed into the life after it.

I held him until his shaking passed, then stayed beside him without asking for more.

He agreed to speak with someone about the nightmares, and I offered to sit beside him while he made the arrangement.

Iroh agreed to seek help for the nightmares. I promised only to sit beside him while he made the call. I sat beside him until he was ready for sleep. I sat beside him until he was ready for sleep.
